title: Lakehouse tables with Apache Iceberg
goal: By the end you can explain why a table format exists, walk an Iceberg table's metadata from the pointer to the Parquet files, describe a commit as a compare-and-swap with retries, and use snapshots, time travel, schema evolution and hidden partitioning from Spark.

warmup.q: A Spark job is writing 200 Parquet files into a Hive-style table folder, `dt=2026-11-07/`. Halfway through, a dashboard query reads that day. What does it see?
options: Nothing from today, because Spark locks the folder while it writes
Whatever files have landed so far: part of the job's rows
All 200 files, because the reader waits for the writer
An error, because the folder is being written
warmup.why: In a folder-as-table, the table is whatever files the folder lists right now, and files land as tasks finish. There's no lock and no wait, so a reader can see part of a write. That's the gap a table format closes: in Iceberg, readers see only files a committed snapshot lists, and a commit becomes visible in one atomic step.

sections.h: A table format keeps the file list in metadata, not in the folder
sections.body:
Lesson 3 (Hive: SQL on files, partitions and the metastore) ended with three cracks in the folder-as-table model. A write is not atomic: a job's files appear one by one, and a reader in the middle sees part of the job. Listing is slow: on S3 a listing returns at most 1,000 names per request, so a partition of 50,000 files takes 50 requests before the first byte of data. And the schema is matched by name or position, so renaming a column means rewriting files or confusing readers. All three come from one decision: the folder's contents are the table.

Version 1: keep a list. Next to the data, write a file that names every data file of the table. Readers read the list instead of listing folders, which fixes the listing cost. But a writer still has to change the list, and a reader can catch the list file half rewritten.

Version 2: never change a file; write a new one. A write first puts its new data files down, which nobody reads because no list names them. Then it writes a complete new list, which also nobody reads yet. Then it switches readers from the old list to the new one in a single step. Before the switch, every reader sees the old table; after it, the new one. Nobody can see half.

That single step needs one small, mutable thing: a **pointer** that says which list is current, and an operation that changes it atomically: a compare-and-swap, which sets the pointer to a new value only if it still holds the value you read. Everything else is immutable files. That's the design of a **table format**: Apache Iceberg, Delta Lake and Apache Hudi all work this way. This lesson uses Iceberg, the one Spark, Trino, Flink, DuckDB and most other engines read and write.

The Try it shows the difference with a reader thread that counts rows while a writer adds 8 files. Copied into a plain Parquet folder one at a time, the way tasks publish their output as they finish, the reader saw 3,000, 5,000, 6,000 and 7,000 rows on the way to 8,000: tables that never existed. Appended to an Iceberg table in three commits of 8 files, the reader saw 0, 8,000, 16,000 and 24,000: whole commits and nothing in between.

Iceberg itself is a specification plus libraries, not a server or an engine. The table is files in your storage, and "the catalog" that holds the pointer can be as simple as a folder, which is what this lesson uses: a Hadoop catalog, where the warehouse is a directory tree on your disk.

try.title: Count rows while a writer adds files
steps: Run `AtomicCommitDemo`. A reader thread counts rows in a loop while the main thread adds files: first to a plain Parquet folder, one file a second, then to an Iceberg table, in three commits.
Predict the set of counts the reader will see in each case.
In the plain-folder case, each file appears whole (it's renamed into place). Why does the reader still see a partial write?

code.title: AtomicCommitDemo.kt

try.expect:
```text
plain folder, 8 files added one by one, the reader saw: [0, 3000, 5000, 6000, 7000, 8000]
Iceberg table, 3 commits of 8 files each, the reader saw: [0, 8000, 16000, 24000]
```

In the plain folder every file landed whole, because it was renamed into place, and the reader still saw partial tables: for a folder-as-table, each new file is visible the moment it lands, and a job of 8 files is 8 separate moments. Which partial counts you catch depends on how fast your machine runs the reader's queries, so your list will differ; the point is that it has values between 0 and 8,000. The Iceberg reader only ever saw multiples of 8,000. Each commit wrote its 8 files first, where no snapshot pointed at them, and then made all of them visible in one swap.

sections.h: Iceberg's metadata is a tree of files that are never edited
sections.body:
Version 2 above had a single list file. Write it as one file and every commit must rewrite the whole list: a table of a million files gets a new million-line file for a commit that adds ten. Iceberg splits the list into a tree, so a commit rewrites only a small top and reuses everything below.

From the top, as the figure shows:

1. The table metadata file, `v4.metadata.json`. JSON, one per version of the table. It holds the schemas (every column with a permanent field id), the partition specs, the table properties, and the list of **snapshots**: the table's versions. Each snapshot has an id, its parent's id, a timestamp, a summary, and the path of its manifest list. One of them is current.
2. The manifest list, one Avro file per snapshot. (Avro is a compact binary format that stores records one after another, with the schema in the file's header.) One row per manifest, with the range of partition values inside it, so a query on one day can skip whole manifests without opening them.
3. The manifests, Avro files with one row per data file: its path, its partition value, its row count, its size, and per-column statistics, including the minimum and maximum of each column. Lesson 4's footer statistics, moved up into the table's metadata, so a reader can skip a file without opening it.
4. The data files: plain Parquet.

A commit that appends 8 files writes 8 data files, one new manifest, one new manifest list that names the new manifest plus all the old ones, and one new metadata file. The old manifests are reused as they are. That's why the snapshots are cheap: snapshot S2 and snapshot S3 share every manifest that didn't change.

A reader walks the tree from the top: pointer, metadata file, current snapshot, its manifest list, the manifests whose partition ranges can match, the data files whose statistics can match. It never lists a folder. In the Try it, a create and three appends left four metadata JSON files (one per version), three manifest lists (one per snapshot), three manifests and nine data files, three days per append. Spark also exposes the tree as metadata tables you can query: `lake.pay.payments.snapshots`, `.manifests`, `.files`, `.history`.

try.title: Walk a real table's metadata tree
steps: Run `MetadataTreeDemo`. It creates `lake.pay.payments` partitioned by day, commits three appends of 1,000 payments, then reads the metadata files straight from disk.
Before reading: how many metadata JSON files will there be after a create and three appends? How many manifests will the current manifest list name?
In the manifest, find the `amount_cents` bounds. Which lesson's skipping do they make possible, without opening the Parquet file?

code.title: MetadataTreeDemo.kt
code.src:
package sfz.bigdata.l09.demo

import org.apache.avro.generic.GenericRecord
import java.io.File
import java.nio.ByteBuffer
import java.nio.ByteOrder

/**
 * Creates an Iceberg table, commits three appends, then walks its metadata tree from disk:
 * version-hint.text, the metadata JSON, the manifest list, and one manifest with its column stats.
 */
fun main() {
    val spark = demoSpark()
    spark.sql("CREATE TABLE lake.pay.payments ($PAYMENT_COLUMNS) USING iceberg PARTITIONED BY (days(created_at))")
    for (b in 0 until 3) payments(spark, b * 1_000L, 1_000).writeTo("lake.pay.payments").append()
    val dir = tableDir("pay", "payments")

    println("metadata/ holds:")
    File(dir, "metadata").listFiles { f -> !f.name.startsWith(".") }!!.sortedBy { it.name }.forEach {
        println("  %-60s %,6d bytes".format(it.name.replace(Regex("[0-9a-f]{8}-[0-9a-f]{4}-[0-9a-f]{4}-[0-9a-f]{4}-[0-9a-f]{12}"), "<uuid>"), it.length()))
    }
    val version = File(dir, "metadata/version-hint.text").readText().trim()
    println("version-hint.text says: $version")

    val meta = json(File(dir, "metadata/v$version.metadata.json"))
    val current = meta.path("current-snapshot-id").asLong()
    println("v$version.metadata.json: format-version ${meta.path("format-version")}, current-snapshot-id $current, " +
        "partition spec ${meta.path("partition-specs")[0].path("fields")}")
    for (s in meta.path("snapshots")) {
        val sum = s.path("summary")
        println("  snapshot %d parent %-20s added %s files, table now %s rows, manifest list %s".format(
            s.path("snapshot-id").asLong(), s.path("parent-snapshot-id").asText("none"),
            sum.path("added-data-files").asText(), sum.path("total-records").asText(),
            File(s.path("manifest-list").asText()).name.take(20) + "..."))
    }

    val list = meta.path("snapshots").first { it.path("snapshot-id").asLong() == current }.path("manifest-list").asText()
    println("the current manifest list names ${avro(list).size} manifests:")
    for (m in avro(list)) {
        println("  %s  added_files %s existing_files %s".format(
            File(m.get("manifest_path").toString()).name.take(14) + "...", m.get("added_files_count"), m.get("existing_files_count")))
    }

    val newest = avro(list).first().get("manifest_path").toString()
    val amountId = meta.path("schemas")[0].path("fields").first { it.path("name").asText() == "amount_cents" }.path("id").asInt()
    println("one manifest, ${avro(newest).size} entries (amount_cents is field $amountId):")
    for (e in avro(newest)) {
        val f = e.get("data_file") as GenericRecord
        @Suppress("UNCHECKED_CAST")
        fun bound(name: String): Long =
            ((f.get(name) as List<GenericRecord>).first { it.get("key") == amountId }.get("value") as ByteBuffer)
                .duplicate().order(ByteOrder.LITTLE_ENDIAN).long
        println("  status %s  %-64s rows %s  amount_cents %,d..%,d".format(
            e.get("status"), rel(dir, f.get("file_path").toString()).replace(Regex("[0-9a-f]{8}-[0-9a-f]{4}-[0-9a-f]{4}-[0-9a-f]{4}-[0-9a-f]{12}"), "<uuid>"),
            f.get("record_count"), bound("lower_bounds"), bound("upper_bounds")))
    }
    spark.stop()
}

sections.h: A commit is one compare-and-swap of the table pointer
sections.body:
Everything in the tree is written once and never changed. The only thing a commit changes is the pointer, and that's where concurrency is handled.

A commit, step by step, as the stepper shows: write the data files; write a manifest for them; write a manifest list for the new snapshot; write the new metadata file, which lists the new snapshot as current and keeps the old ones. Up to here nobody can see anything. Then swap the pointer from the old metadata file to the new one, if and only if it still names the old one. That condition makes the swap a compare-and-swap, and it's the whole commit protocol.

What if two writers start from v7 at once? Both build their new metadata on v7. The first to swap wins and the table moves to v8. The second swap fails, because the pointer no longer says v7. The loser doesn't wait on a lock; it reloads v8, checks that its change still makes sense (for an append, it always does), re-applies it on top of v8, and swaps again. This is **optimistic concurrency**: no locks while working, a check at the end, and a retry when the check fails. Iceberg's docs call the result serializable isolation: all changes form one linear history. The retry is cheap because the data files and the new manifest are reused, and only the small files at the top are written again.

Where the pointer lives depends on the catalog. In the Hadoop catalog of this lesson it's the metadata files themselves: a commit writes `v8.metadata.json` under a temporary name and renames it into place, and the rename fails if `v8` already exists; `version-hint.text` then tells readers where to start. That needs a file system with an atomic rename, which HDFS and your laptop have and S3 doesn't, so production tables use a catalog with a database behind it (lesson 10).

The old snapshots are still in the metadata, and each one still names exactly the files it had. That gives you **time travel**: `SELECT ... FROM t VERSION AS OF <snapshot id>` or `TIMESTAMP AS OF '<time>'` reads the table as it was. Readers also get isolation for free: a query that started on S1 keeps reading S1's files even if S2 commits halfway through. The window ends when old snapshots are expired and their files deleted, a cleanup job lesson 10 covers.

try.title: Lose a commit race, then read the past
steps: Run `CommitDemo`. Two writers load the same table version. Writer A commits a property change with Iceberg's low-level `commit(base, new)`; writer B then tries the same from its stale base. Then B retries through the normal API, and the demo appends twice more and time-travels.
Predict what B's first attempt does, and which metadata file the table ends up at.
Why is the `TIMESTAMP AS OF` count the same as the first snapshot's?

code.title: CommitDemo.kt
code.src:
package sfz.bigdata.l09.demo

import org.apache.iceberg.HasTableOperations
import org.apache.iceberg.TableMetadata
import org.apache.iceberg.exceptions.CommitFailedException
import org.apache.iceberg.hadoop.HadoopTables

/**
 * Two writers start from the same version of a table. The first commit wins the swap; the second
 * is refused, then retried on top of the new version. Then time travel.
 */
fun main() {
    val spark = demoSpark()
    spark.sql("CREATE TABLE lake.pay.ledger ($PAYMENT_COLUMNS) USING iceberg PARTITIONED BY (days(created_at))")
    payments(spark, 0, 1_000).writeTo("lake.pay.ledger").append()
    val firstCommitAt = System.currentTimeMillis()
    Thread.sleep(50)
    val location = tableDir("pay", "ledger").absolutePath
    val tables = HadoopTables(spark.sparkContext().hadoopConfiguration())

    // two writers load the table: both see the same current version
    val tableA = tables.load(location)
    val tableB = tables.load(location)
    val a = (tableA as HasTableOperations).operations()
    val b = (tableB as HasTableOperations).operations()
    val baseA = a.current()
    val baseB = b.current()
    println("writer A and writer B both start from ${baseA.metadataFileLocation().substringAfterLast('/')}")

    // the low-level commit: "replace base with this new metadata", a compare-and-swap
    a.commit(baseA, TableMetadata.buildFrom(baseA).setProperties(mapOf("settlement.run" to "A")).build())
    println("A commits: the table is now at ${a.current().metadataFileLocation().substringAfterLast('/')}")
    try {
        b.commit(baseB, TableMetadata.buildFrom(baseB).setProperties(mapOf("settlement.run" to "B")).build())
    } catch (e: CommitFailedException) {
        println("B commits from the old base: CommitFailedException: ${e.message!!.substringBefore(": /")}")
    }

    // the normal API, on B's same stale table object: it reloads the current version, applies
    // the change to it and swaps; if the swap loses again, it repeats (commit.retry.num-retries)
    tableB.updateProperties().set("settlement.run", "B").commit()
    val now = tables.load(location)
    println("B retries on top of A: the table is at ${(now as HasTableOperations).operations().current().metadataFileLocation().substringAfterLast('/')}, " +
        "settlement.run = ${now.properties()["settlement.run"]}")

    // two more appends, then read the past
    payments(spark, 1_000, 500).writeTo("lake.pay.ledger").append()
    payments(spark, 1_500, 500).writeTo("lake.pay.ledger").append()
    val history = spark.sql("SELECT snapshot_id, parent_id, operation FROM lake.pay.ledger.snapshots ORDER BY committed_at").collectAsList()
    println("snapshots: " + history.joinToString { "${it.getLong(0)} (${it.getString(2)})" })
    println("now: %,d rows".format(spark.table("lake.pay.ledger").count()))
    println("VERSION AS OF the first snapshot: %,d rows".format(
        spark.sql("SELECT count(*) FROM lake.pay.ledger VERSION AS OF ${history.first().getLong(0)}").first().getLong(0)))
    println("TIMESTAMP AS OF just after the first commit: %,d rows".format(
        spark.sql("SELECT count(*) FROM lake.pay.ledger TIMESTAMP AS OF CAST($firstCommitAt / 1000.0 AS TIMESTAMP)").first().getLong(0)))
    spark.stop()
}

sections.h: Columns have ids and partitions are derived from columns
sections.body:
Two more consequences of keeping the truth in metadata: columns can change without rewriting data, and partitions become a property of the table rather than of your queries.

Start with columns. Every column gets a permanent field id when it's created, and Iceberg writes that id into the Parquet files next to the name. Readers match a file's columns to the table's by id. So renaming `amount_cents` to `amount_minor` is a metadata change: the id stays, old files still match, and no data file is touched. Adding a column gives it a new id that no old file has, so old rows read NULL. Dropping a column removes it from the schema, and its data in old files is simply never read again. Iceberg's docs list add, drop, rename, reorder and type widening, all without rewriting files. Compare a folder of Parquet matched by name: drop `amount_cents`, add a new `amount_cents`, and the old values come back from the dead.

Partitions move into the metadata too. Lesson 3's Hive table needed a `dt` string column, and a query that filtered on `created_at` instead of `dt` read every partition. Iceberg partitions by a transform of a real column: `PARTITIONED BY (days(created_at))`, or `hours(...)`, `months(...)`, `bucket(16, merchant_id)`, `truncate(...)`. There's no extra column. Writers compute the partition value, the manifests record it, and a query that filters on `created_at` gets the matching days worked out for it. That's **hidden partitioning**. In the Try it, a one-day filter on `created_at` plans 1 of the 3 data files.

The layout itself can change. When a table outgrows its layout, `ALTER TABLE ... ADD PARTITION FIELD bucket(4, merchant_id)` starts a new partition spec. New files use it, old files keep the spec they were written with, and the planner prunes each group of files with its own spec. Nothing is rewritten.

All of this is format version 2, which Iceberg 1.12 still creates by default. Format version 3 is adopted in the spec, and Iceberg 1.12 with Spark 4.1 can create and write v3 tables. It adds deletion vectors for row-level deletes, the VARIANT type from lesson 8, geometry and geography types, default column values, nanosecond timestamps, and row lineage, a stable `_row_id` for every row. Ask for it with `TBLPROPERTIES ('format-version' = '3')`, as the Try it does, after checking that every engine that reads the table supports v3 and the v3 features you need.

code.src:
package sfz.bigdata.l09.demo

import org.apache.hadoop.fs.Path
import org.apache.iceberg.expressions.Expressions
import org.apache.iceberg.spark.Spark3Util
import org.apache.parquet.hadoop.ParquetFileReader
import org.apache.parquet.hadoop.util.HadoopInputFile
import java.io.File

/**
 * Hidden partitioning, schema evolution and partition evolution on one table, and a format v3
 * table for comparison.
 */
fun main() {
    val spark = demoSpark()
    val name = "lake.pay.evolving"
    spark.sql("CREATE TABLE $name ($PAYMENT_COLUMNS) USING iceberg PARTITIONED BY (days(created_at))")
    payments(spark, 0, 3_000).writeTo(name).append()
    val dir = tableDir("pay", "evolving")
    fun dataFiles() = File(dir, "data").walkTopDown().filter { it.isFile && it.name.endsWith(".parquet") }.toList()
    println("data folders: " + File(dir, "data").list()!!.sorted())

    // hidden partitioning: filter on created_at, and Iceberg works out which day folders can match
    val table = Spark3Util.loadIcebergTable(spark, name)
    val all = table.newScan().planFiles().use { it.count() }
    val nov2 = table.newScan().filter(Expressions.and(
        Expressions.greaterThanOrEqual("created_at", "2026-11-02T00:00:00+00:00"),
        Expressions.lessThan("created_at", "2026-11-03T00:00:00+00:00"))).planFiles().use { it.count() }
    println("WHERE created_at on 2026-11-02 plans $nov2 of $all data files")

    // schema evolution: the Parquet files store a field id next to every column name
    val file = dataFiles().first()
    val footer = ParquetFileReader.open(HadoopInputFile.fromPath(Path(file.absolutePath), spark.sparkContext().hadoopConfiguration())).use { it.footer }
    println("a data file's Parquet schema: " + footer.fileMetaData.schema.toString().replace("\n", " ").replace(Regex(" +"), " "))
    val before = dataFiles().map { it.name }.toSet()
    spark.sql("ALTER TABLE $name RENAME COLUMN amount_cents TO amount_minor")
    spark.sql("ALTER TABLE $name ADD COLUMN risk_score DOUBLE")
    spark.sql("ALTER TABLE $name DROP COLUMN status")
    println("after rename, add and drop: data files rewritten: ${(before - dataFiles().map { it.name }.toSet()).size}")
    println("columns now: " + spark.table(name).columns().joinToString())
    println("first row now: " + spark.table(name).orderBy("payment_id").first())

    // partition evolution: new data also buckets by merchant; old files keep the old layout
    spark.sql("ALTER TABLE $name ADD PARTITION FIELD bucket(4, merchant_id)")
    payments(spark, 3_000, 1_000).withColumnRenamed("amount_cents", "amount_minor").drop("status").writeTo(name).append()
    spark.sql("SELECT spec_id, count(*) AS files, sum(record_count) AS rows FROM $name.files GROUP BY spec_id ORDER BY spec_id").collectAsList()
        .forEach { println("partition spec ${it.getInt(0)}: ${it.getLong(1)} files, ${it.getLong(2)} rows") }
    println("a new data folder: " + dataFiles().map { it.parentFile.relativeTo(File(dir, "data")).path }.filter { "bucket" in it }.sorted().first())

    // the newest format version, for comparison
    spark.sql("CREATE TABLE lake.pay.v3 ($PAYMENT_COLUMNS) USING iceberg TBLPROPERTIES ('format-version' = '3')")
    payments(spark, 0, 100).writeTo("lake.pay.v3").append()
    val v3 = json(File(tableDir("pay", "v3"), "metadata/v2.metadata.json"))
    println("lake.pay.v3: format-version ${v3.path("format-version")}, next-row-id ${v3.path("next-row-id")}")
    println("v3 row lineage: " + spark.sql("SELECT payment_id, _row_id, _last_updated_sequence_number FROM lake.pay.v3 ORDER BY payment_id LIMIT 2").collectAsList())
    spark.stop()
}

Iceberg partitioning: hidden partitioning and transforms

analogy: An Iceberg table works like a Git repository. The Parquet files are blobs: written once, never changed. Each metadata file is a commit: it records the whole state of the table and points back to its parent. The catalog's pointer is the branch ref, `main`, naming the current commit. Writing data is like `git commit`: you create new blobs and a new commit object, and nothing changes for anyone until the ref moves. Moving the ref is a compare-and-swap, like a push that is rejected when someone else pushed first, after which you rebase and push again. Time travel is `git checkout` of an old commit. The analogy breaks at the history: Git keeps every commit forever, while an Iceberg table expires old snapshots on a schedule and deletes the files only they used, so time travel only reaches as far back as the snapshots you kept.
in_your_world: The commit protocol is one you already use. An optimistic lock on your Oracle ledger (`UPDATE accounts SET balance = :b, version = version + 1 WHERE id = :id AND version = :v`, retry if zero rows changed) is the same compare-and-swap Iceberg does on its table pointer. The Kafka log gives you replay by offset; an Iceberg table gives you replay by snapshot, so a nightly reconciliation job can record the snapshot id it read, and an auditor can run the same query against that exact snapshot next month. And the idempotency key on your payment API has a cousin here: Iceberg 1.12 added idempotency keys to the REST catalog protocol, so a writer whose commit request times out can retry without committing the same data twice.
mistake: The common mistake is treating an Iceberg table's folder as the table: listing `data/` to find the files, copying Parquet files into it to "add" data, or deleting files from it to remove a bad day. None of that changes the table, because the table is whatever the current snapshot's manifests list. A copied-in file is invisible to every reader, and a deleted file breaks every snapshot that still lists it, with a missing-file error on the next read. People do it because a Hive table was its folder (lesson 3), and old scripts still treat it that way. Go through the table instead: `INSERT`, `DELETE`, `CALL system.add_files(...)` to register existing files, `CALL system.expire_snapshots(...)` and `remove_orphan_files` to clean up. Let the commit protocol decide what's in the table.

drill.prompt: From memory, write the Spark SQL to: create a payments table partitioned by the day of `created_at` with hidden partitioning; list its snapshots; read it as of a snapshot id; rename `amount_cents` to `amount_minor`; and start bucketing new data by `merchant_id` into 16 buckets. Then say which of the five rewrites a data file.

recap: A table format keeps the list of a table's files in metadata files next to the data, so readers never list folders and a write becomes visible in one step.
Iceberg's metadata is a tree of immutable files: a pointer, a metadata JSON (schemas, partition specs, snapshots), one manifest list per snapshot, manifests with per-file stats, then Parquet files.

A commit writes new files and then swaps the table pointer from the old metadata file to the new one. If someone else swapped first, the writer re-applies its change and tries again: optimistic concurrency.
Every snapshot still lists its files, so `VERSION AS OF` and `TIMESTAMP AS OF` read the past until the snapshot is expired.

Columns are tracked by id, so rename, add and drop are metadata changes. Partitions are transforms of columns (`days(created_at)`), so queries filter on the column and the layout can change without rewriting old files.

quiz.q: A Spark job is halfway through an `INSERT INTO` an Iceberg table when another query reads the table. What does the reader see?
options: The rows from the data files written so far
Nothing new: the new files aren't in any committed snapshot until the pointer swap
An error, because the table is locked during writes
A random mix, depending on which files the reader lists first
quiz.why: Readers find files through the current snapshot's manifests, never by listing folders. The writer's new files exist on disk but no committed snapshot names them until the single pointer swap at the end, so the reader sees the table exactly as it was. Iceberg takes no read locks; the AtomicCommitDemo's reader only ever saw whole commits.

quiz.q: Two jobs append to the same Iceberg table at the same moment, both starting from v7. What happens?
options: The second commit overwrites the first one's snapshot
Both write v8.metadata.json and the table is corrupt
One swap wins and makes v8; the other's swap fails, it re-applies its append on top of v8 and commits v9
The second job waits on a lock until the first finishes
quiz.why: A commit is a compare-and-swap: replace v7 with my new metadata only if the pointer still says v7. The loser gets a commit failure, reloads v8, re-applies its change (for an append, it just adds its manifest again; the data files are reused) and swaps again. That's optimistic concurrency: no lock, a check at the end.

quiz.q: An Iceberg table is `PARTITIONED BY (days(created_at))`. Which query skips the other days' files?
options: `WHERE created_at >= '2026-11-03' AND created_at < '2026-11-04'`
Only `WHERE created_at_day = '2026-11-03'`
Neither, because Iceberg doesn't prune on timestamps
Only a query that names the partition directory
quiz.why: With hidden partitioning, Iceberg knows the partition value is `day(created_at)`, so it turns a range on `created_at` into a range of days and skips manifests and files outside it. Queries filter on the real column; there's no `dt` column to remember, which is the trap lesson 3 showed for Hive tables.

quiz.q: You rename `amount_cents` to `amount_minor`, then add a new column called `amount_cents`. What do rows written before the rename show in the new `amount_cents`?
options: Their old amounts, because the Parquet files still have a column of that name
An error, because the name was already used
NULL, because the new column has a new field id that no old file contains
Zero
quiz.why: Iceberg matches columns to file columns by field id, not by name. The renamed column keeps id 5 (say), and the new `amount_cents` gets a fresh id, so old files have nothing for it and readers return NULL. A system that matched by name, like plain Parquet in a folder, would resurrect the old values under the new column: a quiet correctness bug.

quiz.q: From lesson 3: in a Hive table, a job writes `dt=2026-11-08/` straight to storage and no query finds the data until someone runs `MSCK REPAIR TABLE`. Why can't that happen with an Iceberg table?
options: Iceberg scans the folder on every query
Iceberg tables have no partitions
Iceberg runs MSCK REPAIR automatically after each write
The writer can't produce files without also committing a snapshot that lists them; readers only look at what snapshots list
quiz.why: In Hive the metastore lists partitions and the folder lists files, and the two can disagree. In Iceberg the snapshot is the only list: a writer that goes through the table commits a snapshot that names its files, and files nobody committed are invisible orphans, not hidden data. That's also why copying files into the folder by hand does nothing.

flashcards.front: What are the levels of Iceberg's metadata tree, top to bottom?
flashcards.back: Catalog pointer, table metadata file (`vN.metadata.json`), manifest list (one per snapshot), manifests (one row per data file, with stats), data files.

flashcards.front: What makes an Iceberg commit atomic?
flashcards.back: A single compare-and-swap of the table pointer from the old metadata file to the new one. In a Hadoop catalog that's a rename that fails if the target exists.

flashcards.front: What happens to a writer whose commit loses the swap?
flashcards.back: It reloads the new current metadata, checks its change still makes sense, re-applies it and tries the swap again.
The files listed by that snapshot's manifest list, with that snapshot's schema, as long as the snapshot hasn't been expired.

flashcards.front: Why is renaming a column safe in Iceberg?
flashcards.back: Columns are matched by field id, stored in the Parquet files too, so a rename only changes the name in the metadata.
Partitioning by a transform of a column, such as `days(created_at)` or `bucket(16, merchant_id)`; queries filter on the column and Iceberg derives which partitions can match.

flashcards.front: What did Iceberg format v3 add?
flashcards.back: Deletion vectors, the VARIANT type, geometry and geography types, default column values, row lineage and nanosecond timestamps.

terms.plain: A specification for metadata files that list a table's data files, schema and history, so engines can read and commit to it safely.
The complete set of a table's data files at one commit, with an id, a parent and a summary.
An Avro file listing data files with their partition values, row counts and per-column min and max.
An Avro file per snapshot listing its manifests, with the range of partition values in each.
Writers work without locks and check at commit time that nobody changed the table; if someone did, they retry.
Partition values computed from a column by a transform, so queries never name a partition column.
The permanent number Iceberg gives each column; files store it, so names can change safely.

explain_back.prompt: Explain to a colleague who knows Hive tables why an Iceberg `INSERT` is all-or-nothing for readers, using the files the commit writes and the order it writes them in.
explain_back.answer: A Hive table is its folder: whatever files are in `dt=2026-11-03/` right now are the table, so a reader that lists the folder halfway through a write sees half the write. An Iceberg table is whatever its current snapshot lists, and readers find files only through that list. A commit writes in a fixed order. First the new Parquet data files, which no snapshot names yet, so nobody can see them. Then a manifest listing those files with their partition values and stats, then a new manifest list naming the old manifests plus the new one, then a new metadata file that adds the snapshot and makes it current. Up to here, every reader still opens the old metadata file and sees the old table. The last step is one atomic swap of the table pointer from the old metadata file to the new one; in a Hadoop catalog that's a rename that fails if the target exists, in a REST or JDBC catalog a compare-and-swap in the catalog. A reader that starts before the swap sees the old snapshot, one that starts after sees the new one, and none can see a mix. If the job dies before the swap, the files it wrote are orphans that no snapshot lists, cleaned up later, and the table never changed.

deeper.body:
The Hadoop catalog used in this lesson is the simplest catalog, and it's for learning and for HDFS. It relies on the file system's rename failing when the target exists; Iceberg's documentation for `HadoopCatalog` says the file system must support atomic rename, which object stores like S3 don't offer. Production tables use a catalog that keeps the pointer in a database and does the compare-and-swap there: the Hive metastore, a JDBC catalog, AWS Glue, or a REST catalog server such as Apache Polaris. Lesson 10 covers catalogs and the REST protocol.

Old snapshots cost storage: every file any kept snapshot lists stays on disk. `CALL system.expire_snapshots(...)` removes old snapshots from the metadata and deletes the files only they used, and the time travel window ends there. Small appends also pile up small files and small manifests; `rewrite_data_files` and `rewrite_manifests` compact them in a new commit. Lesson 10 covers both, along with row-level deletes and updates.

Format versions: v1 described append-only analytic tables; v2 added row-level deletes with delete files; v3, now adopted, adds binary deletion vectors, the VARIANT type (the same one Spark 4 has, lesson 8), geometry and geography types, default column values, row lineage (`_row_id`, `_last_updated_sequence_number`) and nanosecond timestamps. Iceberg 1.12 still creates v2 tables unless you set `'format-version' = '3'`, as the EvolutionDemo does. Version 4 is in development; its draft replaces the manifest list with a root manifest in an adaptive tree, so a small commit writes fewer metadata files.
